extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/classics; educated general readers interested in Plato
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and objections for judging the plausibility, morality, and consequences of Plato's ideal State as presented in the Republic and Laws. Focuses on practical realizability, social institutions (property, marriage, family), education, and human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal versus practicable realisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing actually existing in the world at all resembles Plato’s ideal State; nor does he himself imagine that such a State is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato treats the Republic as a pattern or vision rather than a literal program to be implemented; he repeatedly admits impossibility (Republic, Laws), argues that ideals are none the worse because they cannot be realized, and answers sceptics ironically (e.g. 'When one son of a king becomes a philosopher'). The evaluator should note whether a proposal is intended as a practical scheme or an illustrative ideal and judge it accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of goods (property arrangements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The community of goods (chiefly among the guardians) — does communal ownership repress industry and benevolence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's and modern critiques contend communal property tends to remove incentives for exertion and weaken benevolent feeling. Historical examples (tribal/common land, early Christian communities) show variety; assess effects on production, dispute, and social welfare as well as whether property rights are justified by expediency rather than sacrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of private property as expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of private property is based on expediency and may be interfered with for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property's sacredness varies by age and society; ancient instability of property and examples (communal land, storage practices) suggest the institution is not absolute. Evaluate proposals by examining whether alternative vesting of property could become legitimate through proven advantage and public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of social arrangements on industry and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Would communal arrangements remove motives for exertion, leading to decreased production and disputes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common objection (Aristotle): removing private ownership represses industry and benevolence. Consider empirical/historical evidence of productivity under communal regimes and weigh risks of free-riding or reduced effort against potential social benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of sexes in training and occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal that occupations of men and women shall be the same, with common training and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato argues natural gifts are scattered indifferently between sexes (though degrees may differ); counterarguments stress pervasive differences (sensibility, gentleness) and the role of education and custom. Evaluation should consider which differences are innate versus socially conditioned and whether equal training is feasible or desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of wives and children (family arrangements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s proposal for common wives and children — is it possible or desirable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major objections: destruction of parental affection and family bonds; reduction of marriage to a breeding arrangement; loss of poetry, love, and higher feelings. Note Plato’s aim (improving the race) and contrast with modern/Christian values that emphasize individual worth and parental ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of higher human qualities versus animalistic selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the proposal neglect imagination, feeling, and higher qualities by treating people like animals to be bred?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue Plato's breeding/selective proposals focus on physical/animal traits and ignore mind, imagination, and moral worth. Evaluate whether any social engineering preserves or destroys higher human qualities and the cultural goods they produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral value of the individual and treatment of the weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether proposals respect the individual worth of the weakest (infant, criminal, insane) as a moral imperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a Christian/modern viewpoint, honouring the weakest is a supreme moral duty; assess whether reforms sacrifice intrinsic respect for individuals in pursuit of collective improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency of the philosophical scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Plato's proposals are internally consistent or self-contradictory (e.g., mixing idealism and crude animalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Plato 'flies and walks at the same time' and sometimes contradicts himself; evaluators should check for logical coherence between principles (e.g., valuing reason while reducing persons to breeding stock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of analogy with animals and 'breeding' arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriateness of reasoning from animal breeding or primitive tribes to human social institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against uncritical inference from animal behaviour or barbarous customs to human society: human moral, imaginative, and social dimensions may make such analogies misleading. Use anthropological evidence cautiously and acknowledge fragmentary records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and power of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education as an ever-multiplying force that can transform society if made universal and rightly adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s picture of education 'moving like a wheel with an ever-multiplying rapidity' recommends assessing proposed institutions by their educational implications: can education instil needed virtues and enable societal change over generations?

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate and plausibility of social change
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether large-scale changes in property, family, or other institutions are realistic within historical rates of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay references historic transformations (emancipation of serfs, abolition of slavery, Japan’s rapid change) to argue that profound change is possible though not guaranteed. Evaluate proposals with appropriate historical perspective on feasible timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity and social function of marriage and family
rubrics_metrics.description: The family as a religious/customary institution that binds members and serves social ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s hostile view of the family as enemy of the state is contrasted with traditions that consecrate marriage; assess whether reforms preserve social cohesion and the beneficial functions of the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical assessment of selective breeding and eugenic measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal to select the best for breeding and destroy the others to improve the race—are such measures morally permissible or effective?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong objections include moral horror, unpredictable inheritance, loss of valued personalities, and historic evidence that great individuals often come from unremarkable parentage. Evaluate both ethical costs and scientific uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygamy versus monogamy and demographic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical claim that widespread polygamy correlates with degeneracy/deterioration of the race, whereas monogamy became dominant in civilized peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical and comparative evidence to weigh social and demographic consequences of different marriage regimes; exceptions exist but are taken as proving the general rule in the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of bodily health and moral/mental health
rubrics_metrics.description: Health of body and mind are interdependent; moral duty and love of truth are essential to true health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that reduce virtue to mere physical health are inadequate; evaluate proposals for whether they cultivate conscience, duty, and intellect as well as bodily wellbeing.
